justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modest upward drift from what appeared to be a baseline price around 222–223, with each successive horizon incorporating slightly more expected appreciation. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and limited overnight catalysts would keep movement tight. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the forecast marginally higher, reflecting a slight positive drift assumption consistent with broader equity market trends. At the one-month horizon, the 226 estimate incorporated a continuation of that drift while acknowledging that compounding small daily moves over roughly 20 trading sessions could accumulate to a modest gain, consistent with historical average monthly returns for large-cap equities or index-related instruments.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to scale with the square root of time, a standard approach grounded in the idea that uncertainty compounds as the forecast horizon extends. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 4.6 points reflects relatively low realized volatility expectations — consistent with an annualized volatility somewhere in the 15–20% range. By one week, the interval widens to about plus or minus 9 points, and by one month it expands to roughly plus or minus 18 points, each reflecting the accumulation of daily variance over longer periods. I also gave slightly fatter tails implicitly by using a wider-than-normal distribution assumption, acknowledging that financial returns tend to exhibit excess kurtosis.

Several sources of uncertainty influenced these widths beyond pure statistical volatility. Macroeconomic data releases — such as employment reports, inflation prints, or central bank communications — can produce outsized single-day moves that would stress even the one-day interval. Earnings announcements, if the underlying asset is a single stock, represent an additional discrete jump risk. At the one-month horizon, the accumulation of geopolitical developments, shifts in monetary policy expectations, or sector-specific news could collectively drive outcomes well outside my stated range.

Specific tail risks that could push outcomes outside my intervals include an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a significant credit event or liquidity shock in financial markets, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions that triggers broad risk-off selling. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as stronger-than-expected economic data, a positive resolution of a trade or geopolitical dispute, or a large short-squeeze dynamic — could push prices well above the upper bound of my one-month range. I would emphasize that stated 90% confidence intervals by construction leave a 10% probability of outcomes outside those bounds, and in practice fat-tailed financial returns make exceedances more common than a Gaussian model would suggest.
